Why Japan's game industry is falling behind

There's something that many people don't get about Japan. Even with it's high tech stuff, there are a lot of things that "stay". I want to say it's like a tradition addiction. When certain tech hits the market it doesn't get phased out as soon as something better comes along like you see in other countries. People like it just as it is and don't care for the "next big thing". You can still buy walkmans, watch things on tape. You can still buy new games for the PS2. Heck, even for the bloody SNES.

The reason they hit the video game market so well originally was because of the lack of competition/inspiration from other countries at the time. Other countries that are more obsessed with updating but didn't see video games as anything beyond just minority entertainment. But that has changed so the tables have turned. It's this lifestyle that Nintendo breathes and why outsiders are wondering what they hell they are thinking. Japan first, rest of the world later. It worked well before, why not again?

Hiroaki Yura explains part of the problem with this slow change (game engines). But he doesn't go into the depth of it because it's super cultural and would require paragraphs and paragraphs to explain the why.

Cell phone games have always, always been a thing in Japan. Pokémon Crystal had a feature with your cellphone which got you the legendary Celebi (children having cellphones was already normal in 90's Japan). However cellphones were not a thing outside of Japan at that time so they removed that feature.

Those games for the most part weren't stupid simple either (at least, the experience of what my friends tell me, as I live in an area of no cell service so that stuff in general is foreign to me). The problem comes from companies deciding to pander to the lowest common denominator. It doesn't have to be that way, but doing less work and being paid more for it is a very tempting lifestyle to possess.

If you wanted to try Ubuntu I would recommend wubi which installs Ubuntu like an application but allows you to dual boot. If you want to try or a different flavor of linux then you have to do the following:

  1. Use windows disk utility to partition your drive and give yourself ~50GB of space (20 is the minimum but you should use more)
  2. Download the ISO of whatever distribution you want and copy it to a flash drive (there are multiple utilities for this, or if you have a mac computer somewhere you can use the dd command)
  3. Live-boot to the USB
  4. Install to the partition you created (depending on which flavor of linux you went with this is probably graphical)
  5. Reboot and go into Linux

Notes to consider:

  1. You will probably install GRUB as the boot manager. These days it will probably auto-detect your windows partition but just in case read the documentation first.
  2. If you get stuck the Arch Wiki is excellent for all things Linux. You're probably not using Arch, but the wiki is some of the best documentation on most problems or software you may run into.

Easiest way is with two HDDs. Install one OS on one drive, install the other OS on the other. Hold F8 during boot to choose which OS to boot to. No boot manager needed.

EDIT: Actually easiest way is Ubuntu with wubi: Download the latest image from their website, burn or mount the image, copy just the install exe to your desktop, run and follow the instructions. It installs/uninstalls just like any other application, you don't even need to partition your drive and can use a dynamic image for your Ubuntu install that expands as needed.

Partition your hard drive. (you probably already have a C: partition, you want to make a second letter to put your other OS on). Boot from your install media (flash drive, dvd etc) When it asks where you want the OS to be installed to, pick the new partition you made as the install location. The rest you should be able to figure out pretty easily.

Alternatively to what some are saying here, if you have a decent amount of RAM available (8+ GB generally) and you don't require true native performance from the secondary OSes you can use some virtualization layer such as Virtualbox (free).

For example, if you have Windows 7 as your primary (host) OS and you want to try Ubuntu Linux out, you can download the Ubuntu .iso file, mount and install that using Virtualbox and dedicate maybe 40+ GB hard drive space, 4 GB of RAM, 1 or 2 cores/cpus, and varying levels of video memory to this Linux "guest" system... then you have Linux running inside a window (sorta like an application) on top of Windows. You can even set it up to drag and drop files between the two and share folders, clilboard, etc. This setup can also protect you by adding an additional sandbox layering so if you, say, download some malware inside the guest system it won't necessarily infect the underlying host (although it can, especially if it spreads via shared folders, clipboard, and/or network bridge ... so don't think it is fool proof). However, you probably wouldn't want to use this guest for anything that is too resource/performance dependent like gaming, video editing, etc as the added overhead and abstraction layering is not going to give you the same performance you'd expect from a native, host system.

I installed Ubuntu LTS 12.04 Precise Pangolin on my Windows 7 machine earlier this year. These are the instructions I used. I consider myself a fairly computer-smart person, but this was my first foray into dualbooting and Linux.

Basic rundown of what I did:

  • Burn an Ubuntu live CD. There are tons of guides on how to do this online.

  • Boot from live CD into Ubuntu and run GParted. Partition the HDD manually as per the guide, making sure to create the correct tyopes of partitions with the right type of filesystem for each (not NTFS).

  • Run the Ubuntu installer (watch that it installs on the right partition).

  • Fix the boot loader. This was the most difficult part for me as I didn't really understand what I was doing, but then, I didn't really understand any of this, and was just flying by the seat of my pants. I ran through the instructions on that linked guide above and wasn't happy with the result after allowing Windows to fix its master boot record (MBR) and then installing GRUB. The only problem for me was that once Windows fixed its MBR, I couldn't access Ubuntu. I installed 3rd party software in Windows called EasyBCD which allowed me to change my MBR via a GUI. It worked.

The end result was a computer which, when booted, displayed the GRUB screen. The first entry was Windows, the second was Ubuntu. Booting into Ubuntu booted Ubuntu right off the bat, whereas booting into Windows brought up the MBR screen instead of booting straight into Windows. This didn't matter to me though, because either way, give it approx 5 seconds and it booted into the chosen OS without further interaction.

Good luck!
